fix: close Cognito self-signup + gate the generic-OIDC path on an allowlist (#1385)

A valid token from the configured issuer was sufficient to be auto-provisioned
a DataQ account (`_upsert_user`), so the IdP's own registration policy silently
became DataQ's access policy. The AWS deployment's Cognito pool shipped with
self-service sign-up ENABLED and its hosted UI served a working /signup form to
anyone who found the domain — verified live — so any stranger could register,
verify their own email, and land an authenticated account in the workspace.

That also dissolved the "single-tenant, workspace-trusted" premise that #1118
(arbitrary `*_secret_name` resolution -> warehouse-credential exfiltration) is
deliberately accepted under, turning a known internal risk into a remotely
reachable one.

Two layers:

- IdP (the actual fix): `allow_admin_create_user_only = true` on the pool.
  Operators are admin-created; /signup stops serving a form; existing users are
  unaffected.
- App: OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS / OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, so the same mistake in any
  issuer's console cannot reach the database. Checked on every request rather
  than only at insert, so removing an entry also revokes an existing account.

Empty allowlist = admit everyone, which is the pre-existing behaviour and stays
the default deliberately: fail-closed here would turn a routine image bump into
a workspace-wide lockout. `init_auth()` logs `auth_oidc_no_signup_allowlist` at
WARNING in that state so "open" is visible rather than silent.

Both generic-OIDC dependencies had byte-identical bodies; they now share one
`_resolve_generic_oidc_user` so the gate cannot be added to one and missed on
the other. The OTP and OIDC allowlists were also folded onto two shared parsing
helpers — one normalization rule on the identity surface (ADR 0032 decision 6).

Tests verified against the unfixed code: all 6 denial cases fail without the
gate, for the right reason.

Azure is unaffected — the AAD tenant is the gate there.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

# Security response headers (#1386) — included from nginx.conf.template.
#
# WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE FILE, and why it is `include`d more than once:
# nginx's `add_header` is inherited from an outer level ONLY when the current
# level declares no `add_header` of its own. Three of this server's locations
# set their own `Cache-Control`, so a single server-level block here would be
# silently dropped in exactly those locations — including `location /`, which
# serves index.html and is the one response where `frame-ancestors` and the CSP
# actually matter. Repeating the block via `include` is nginx's own idiom for
# that; there is no inheritance-safe alternative in stock nginx (`more_set_headers`
# needs the third-party headers-more module).
#
# This file lives at /etc/nginx/ and NOT in /etc/nginx/conf.d/, deliberately:
# everything in conf.d is auto-included into `http {}`, which would emit every
# header a second time.
#
# `always` on every line so the headers ride error responses too (403/404/5xx) —
# a 403 from the origin-secret guard is still a document a browser will render.

# Clickjacking. `frame-ancestors` in the CSP below is the modern control and
# supersedes this, but X-Frame-Options is what pre-CSP3 browsers honour.
add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;

# Stop content-type sniffing. Matters most on /assets/* — a JS bundle mislabelled
# by an upstream proxy must not be re-interpreted as something executable.
add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;

# Don't leak in-app paths (which carry run/suite/asset UUIDs) to third parties
# via Referer, while keeping same-origin referrers intact for our own navigation.
add_header Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" always;

# DataQ asks for none of these. Explicitly denying them means an injected iframe
# or script cannot ask on our origin's behalf.
add_header Permissions-Policy "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=(), usb=()" always;

# HSTS. Ignored by browsers on a plain-HTTP origin, so this is inert on the
# compose stack and active behind CloudFront / ACA ingress — one image, both.
# `preload` is deliberately NOT set: submitting a *.cloudfront.net or
# *.azurecontainerapps.io host to the preload list is not ours to do, and it is
# effectively irreversible.
add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;

# CSP, assembled in nginx.conf.template (it needs runtime env). nginx omits an
# `add_header` whose value evaluates to the empty string, so setting
# DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC/... such that $dataq_csp is empty is a supported way to
# turn the policy off without a rebuild.
add_header Content-Security-Policy $dataq_csp always;

content.text: Now the CSP assembly and the `include` calls in the template:

input.new_string:
map $http_x_forwarded_proto $dataq_forwarded_proto {
    default $http_x_forwarded_proto;
    ""      $scheme;
}

# ── Content-Security-Policy (#1386) ───────────────────────────────────────────
# Assembled here rather than in nginx-security-headers.conf because the one part
# that cannot be static is `connect-src`: the SPA's OIDC client fetches discovery,
# JWKS and the token endpoint directly from the identity provider, and which
# origins those are is a per-deployment runtime fact (ADR 0028 — one generic
# image, nothing baked in).
#
# `DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC` is the whole tail of the connect-src list. It defaults
# to `https:` in the Dockerfile, NOT to the empty string, and that default is
# load-bearing: a BYO deployment that upgrades this image without setting the
# variable must not have its sign-in silently broken by a policy it never opted
# into. Deployments we control set explicit origins instead (both Terraform
# stacks do), which is what actually makes the directive worth having.
#
# It cannot be derived from DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY, which is why it is a separate
# variable: an authority is a URL *with a path* (`…/<tenant>/v2.0` on Azure AD),
# a CSP source matches by path prefix, and Azure's token endpoint sits at
# `…/<tenant>/oauth2/v2.0/token` — outside that prefix. Deriving it would have
# produced a policy that blocked the token exchange on exactly one cloud.
#
# Keyed on $host purely because `map` requires a source variable; the result is
# the same for every host.
map $host $dataq_csp {
    default "default-src 'self'; base-uri 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self'; img-src 'self' data: blob:; font-src 'self' data:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self'; worker-src 'self' blob:; connect-src 'self' ${DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC}";
}

{ name = "DATAQ_AUTH_LOGOUT_STYLE", value = "cognito" },
        # CSP connect-src tail (#1386). BOTH Cognito hosts are required and they
        # are different services: oidc-client-ts fetches discovery + JWKS from
        # the ISSUER host (cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com) and then POSTs the
        # code exchange to the HOSTED-UI domain (<prefix>.auth.<region>.
        # amazoncognito.com). Omitting the second one yields a policy that passes
        # discovery and then blocks the token exchange — i.e. sign-in fails at
        # the last step, which is the least obvious way for this to break.
        {
          name = "DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC",
          value = join(" ", [
            "https://cognito-idp.${var.aws_region}.amazonaws.com",
            "https://${aws_cognito_user_pool_domain.app.domain}.auth.${var.aws_region}.amazoncognito.com",
          ])
        },
      ]

advertised its exact nginx build.

The trap this had to work around: nginx drops every inherited `add_header` at
any level that declares one of its own. Three locations here set their own
Cache-Control, including `location /` — the one that serves index.html. A
single server-level block would therefore have been silently absent from
exactly the response where frame-ancestors and the CSP matter, and would have
looked completely correct in the config. Hence the shared snippet, re-included
in each shadowing location. Proven empirically, not assumed: with the
`location /` re-include removed, index.html gets 0 security headers while the
server-level include is still present; restored, it gets them.

CSP connect-src is assembled from DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC rather than derived
from DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY: an authority carries a path (`/<tenant>/v2.0` on
Azure AD), CSP sources match by path prefix, and Azure's token endpoint sits
outside that prefix — deriving it would have passed discovery and then blocked
the code exchange. Both Terraform stacks now set explicit origins (AWS needs
BOTH Cognito hosts: issuer for discovery/JWKS, hosted-UI domain for the token
POST). The image default is `https:`, not empty, so a BYO deployment upgrading
this image doesn't get its sign-in broken by a policy it never opted into.

config (Vite dev server never exercises this path): OTP sign-in, dashboard,
results, assets, connections, suites, admin, profile, settings — 0 violations;
Monaco mounts and renders under `script-src 'self'`; same-origin module
workers, blob workers and blob download URLs all allowed. Negative controls
confirm the policy is actually enforced rather than merely present: inline
script, CDN script and cross-origin fetch are all blocked.

`waf.tf` attaches a WAFv2 Web ACL to the distribution with two rules: a per-IP
rate ceiling (`waf_rate_limit_per_5min`, default 2000 per 5 min) and an
oversized-body block (`waf_max_body_bytes`, default 8KB).

Found in the 2026-08-16 security-surface audit of both deployments (items 1–3 of that audit shipped as #1385/#1386/#1387; this is item 4).

## Finding

The AWS deployment terminates TLS at CloudFront and then talks to the ALB over **plain HTTP**:

- `deploy/terraform/aws/cloudfront.tf` — `origin_protocol_policy = "http-only"`
- `deploy/terraform/aws/alb.tf` — the listener is `port = 80, protocol = "HTTP"`

Both files already document this honestly. Recording it as a tracked item rather than leaving it as prose in a comment.

Consequences:

1. **The edge→origin leg is readable to an on-path observer inside AWS.** That includes the `X-DataQ-Origin-Secret` header (#1355) and every session bearer/cookie. The adversary class that can observe that hop already sees the full session traffic, so this is not a new capability for them — but it does mean the origin secret is not a secret against them, which is exactly the property #1355 exists to provide.
2. **HSTS (added in #1386) cannot be honoured end-to-end.** It protects viewer→CloudFront, which is the leg that matters most, but the deployment cannot claim full HTTPS transport.

Azure is not affected in the same way: the frontend→api hop is `allow_insecure_connections` HTTP but never leaves the Container Apps environment, whereas the CloudFront→ALB hop crosses the AWS network.

## Root cause

No custom domain. Without one there is no ACM certificate the ALB could serve, so the origin cannot speak HTTPS with a verifiable name.

## Fix

Single change with several payoffs:

1. Choose a domain; Route53 hosted zone.
2. ACM cert (us-east-1 for the CloudFront alias, plus a regional cert for the ALB).
3. Add `aliases` + `viewer_certificate` to the distribution.
4. ALB: add a 443 listener with the regional cert; flip `origin_protocol_policy` to `https-only`.
5. Update the Cognito callback/logout URLs and `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` to the new host.

Also unblocks HSTS `preload`, which #1386 deliberately omitted because submitting a `*.cloudfront.net` host to the preload list is not ours to do.

## Acceptance

- `curl -sI https://<domain>/` returns the app; direct-to-ALB over :80 no longer serves.
- The origin fetch is HTTPS (verify from an ALB access log entry or CloudFront's own `cs-protocol` field).
- Sign-in still completes end-to-end (Cognito redirect URIs must be updated in the same change or login breaks).

Referenced from the known-gaps list in `deploy/terraform/aws/README.md`.

gh issue create --title "security: ElastiCache at-rest encryption disabled; ECS/RDS/ElastiCache sit in public subnets with unrestricted egress" --label security --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Found in the 2026-08-16 security-surface audit of both deployments (item 5). Two related AWS network/storage posture gaps, both verified live.

## 1. ElastiCache at-rest encryption is OFF

```
$ aws elasticache describe-replication-groups --replication-group-id dataq-app \
    --query 'ReplicationGroups[0].{tls:TransitEncryptionEnabled,auth:AuthTokenEnabled,atRest:AtRestEncryptionEnabled}'
{ "tls": true, "auth": true, "atRest": false }
```

`transit_encryption_enabled` and `auth_token` are both set in `deploy/terraform/aws/elasticache.tf`; `at_rest_encryption_enabled` is simply absent, so it defaults off. RDS by contrast has `storage_encrypted = true`.

What is actually in Redis: Celery task payloads (suite/run UUIDs and task kwargs) and ADR 0035 rate-limit counters. Low sensitivity, but the fix is free and it is an odd asymmetry against the encrypted RDS beside it.

**Fix:** `at_rest_encryption_enabled = true`. Note this forces **replacement** of the replication group — fine for a broker with no persistence, but it means a short Celery outage, so pair it with a deploy window.

## 2. Everything is in public subnets with unrestricted egress

`deploy/terraform/aws/main.tf` documents the no-NAT decision (saves ~$33/mo) and it is a legitimate MVP tradeoff. Verified that **inbound is genuinely closed** — ECS tasks carry public IPs but the SG has no `0.0.0.0/0` ingress, and probing the api task's public IP on :8000 times out; RDS is `publicly_accessible: false` and resolves to a private address. So this is not an exposure today.

The gap is **egress**: every task can reach any host on the internet (`egress { protocol = "-1", cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"] }` on all three SGs). That is the exfiltration path for the credential-disclosure class in #1118, and nothing constrains it. It is also what makes an SSRF from a connection config reach an arbitrary attacker endpoint.

**Fix options, cheapest first:**
- Keep public subnets but replace blanket egress with an allowlist (443 to the warehouse endpoints + AWS service endpoints). Free, but needs the real egress set enumerated first.
- VPC endpoints for the AWS services in use (Secrets Manager, ECR/GHCR is external, CloudWatch, SES) — removes some internet dependence without a NAT.
- Full private subnets + NAT — correct, ~$33/mo.

## Acceptance

- `AtRestEncryptionEnabled: true` on the replication group, worker reconnects, a suite run completes.
- Egress: a documented decision recorded either way — either the allowlist lands, or the blanket rule stays with the reasoning captured next to #1118 (which is the thing it makes worse).

Related: #1118 (arbitrary `*_secret_name` resolution — the exfiltration this egress rule enables), #1384 (cleartext origin hop).
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

Found in the 2026-08-16 security-surface audit. **Live-exploitable on the AWS deployment at time of filing.** Fixed in the same session — see the linked PR.

## Finding

`AllowAdminCreateUserOnly` was `false` on the Cognito pool, and the hosted UI served a working sign-up form:

```
GET https://dataq-app-<prefix>.auth.us-east-2.amazoncognito.com/signup?client_id=...
=> 200, <form>, "Sign up", name="password"
```

DataQ auto-provisions a user row for any identity the configured issuer vouches for (`_upsert_user`, `backend/app/core/auth.py`) with **no app-side gate** on the generic-OIDC path. So the IdP's registration policy silently *was* DataQ's access policy: register → verify your own email → authenticated account inside the workspace.

MFA was also `OFF` and no advanced-security add-ons were enabled.

## Why it mattered beyond "an extra account"

It dissolved the premise #1118 is deliberately accepted under. That issue (arbitrary `*_secret_name` resolution → SSRF + warehouse-credential exfiltration) is triaged as tolerable because DataQ is single-tenant and *workspace-trusted* — i.e. the risk is bounded to authenticated insiders. With open registration, "any authenticated user" meant "anyone on the internet", making a known internal risk remotely reachable:

1. Self-register.
2. Read a victim connection's `catalog_secret_name` from `GET /connections` (connection-unscoped by design).
3. `POST /connections/test` with `catalog_uri` pointed at an attacker host + the victim's secret name.
4. Server resolves the real credential and sends it out.

## Not affected

Azure. The AAD tenant is the gate there — guests must be invited.

## Fix

- `allow_admin_create_user_only = true` on the pool (the real fix — blocks it at the IdP).
- `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS` / `OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` as a second, app-side layer, checked on every request so it also revokes.

Empty allowlist stays "admit everyone" deliberately — a fail-closed default would turn a routine image bump into a workspace-wide lockout — but `init_auth()` now logs `auth_oidc_no_signup_allowlist` at WARNING in that state.

## Follow-up worth considering

MFA is still off. Not blocking for a demo-scoped deployment with an invite-only pool, but worth a decision.
EOF

Verified live against **both** clouds — the full response header set on `/` was:

```

content-type: text/html
cache-control: no-cache
etag / last-modified / accept-ranges

No `Content-Security-Policy`, `Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Frame-Options`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy` or `Permissions-Policy`. A repo-wide grep found no such header defined anywhere in the codebase. The nginx version was also disclosed.

nginx drops every inherited `add_header` at any level that declares one of its own. A single server-level block would therefore have been **silently absent from exactly the response where `frame-ancestors` and the CSP matter**, while looking entirely correct in the config file.

Proven rather than assumed: with the `location /` re-include removed and the server-level include still present, index.html receives 0 security headers; restored, it receives them.

A shared snippet (`frontend/nginx-security-headers.conf`) re-included in each shadowing location, plus `server_tokens off`. CSP `connect-src` is runtime-configured via `DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC` (both Terraform stacks set explicit IdP origins) rather than derived from `DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY` — an authority carries a path, CSP matches by path prefix, and Azure AD's token endpoint sits outside it, so deriving it would have passed discovery then blocked the code exchange.

Verified in a real browser against the real built bundle behind the real nginx config, with negative controls confirming the policy is enforced and not merely present.

## Deliberately not included

`preload` on HSTS — submitting a `*.cloudfront.net` / `*.azurecontainerapps.io` host to the preload list is not ours to do and is effectively irreversible. Revisit with #1384 (custom domain).
EOF

Found in the 2026-08-16 security-surface audit. Fixed in the same session — see the linked PR.

## Finding

DDoS was the weakest part of the posture on both clouds.

**AWS.** The distribution ran `Managed-CachingDisabled` on *every* path, so CloudFront was a pure pass-through: every request — including all static assets on every page load — reached the origin. The "CDN" in front of the app absorbed nothing, so a flood and a legitimate page load cost the origin the same. No WAF was attached. Behind it: three ECS services at `desired_count = 1` with no autoscaling.

**Azure.** No Front Door / WAF at all; api scales to max 3 replicas and the worker is pinned at 1.

**Both.** The only rate limiting was the app's own (ADR 0035), which:
- counts in Redis *inside* the request path, so a rejected request has already paid the full CloudFront → ALB → nginx → FastAPI hop, and
- **fails open** by design, with a 5s breaker — so the pressure most likely to stress Redis is exactly the pressure that switches enforcement off.

That is the right availability trade for the app limiter, but it left no layer shedding load before the origin.

Verified live that the limiter itself does enforce under normal conditions (150-request burst → 60× 429 on AWS, 32× 429 on Azure), so this is about the missing outer layer, not a broken inner one.

## Fix (AWS)

- WAFv2 Web ACL on the distribution: per-IP rate ceiling (2000 / 5 min — an order of magnitude above the app's 120/min unauthenticated class, so it catches floods without shaping traffic) + an 8KB oversized-body block. Aggregated on the viewer IP, not `FORWARDED_IP`: nothing sits in front of the edge, so trusting a forwarded header there would let an attacker pick their own bucket.
- `/assets/*` cache behavior so the edge actually absorbs the bulk of a page load. Safe only because filenames are content-hashed; `/api/*`, `/mcp` and `index.html` still reach the origin every time.

Two rules, no managed rule groups — those are $10–20/mo each and this deployment is cost-sensitive. Total ~$7/mo; `waf_enabled = false` removes it.

Three fixes from a security-surface audit of the Azure and AWS deployments. Every claim below was verified against the **running** deployments, not read off the IaC.

## #1386 — Cognito self-signup was open (live-exploitable)

`AllowAdminCreateUserOnly` was `false` and the hosted UI served a working sign-up form. DataQ auto-provisions an account for any identity the issuer vouches for, with no app-side gate — so the pool's registration policy *was* the product's access policy: register, verify your own email, land inside the workspace.

It also dissolved the "single-tenant, workspace-trusted" premise #1118 is accepted under, making that credential-exfiltration path remotely reachable rather than insider-only.

- `allow_admin_create_user_only = true` (the real fix, at the IdP).
- `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS` / `OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` as a second app-side layer, checked on **every** request so it revokes as well as grants.
- Empty allowlist stays "admit everyone" deliberately — fail-closed would make a routine image bump a workspace-wide lockout — but `init_auth()` now logs `auth_oidc_no_signup_allowlist` at WARNING in that state.
- Both generic-OIDC dependencies had byte-identical bodies; they now share one `_resolve_generic_oidc_user`, so the gate can't be added to one and missed on the other.

Azure is unaffected (the AAD tenant is the gate).

## #1387 — no security response headers on either cloud

Confirmed live: no CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy or Permissions-Policy anywhere, plus nginx version disclosure.

The subtle part: nginx drops inherited `add_header` at any level declaring its own, and three locations set `Cache-Control` — including `location /`, which serves index.html. A single server-level block would have been silently absent from exactly the response that needs it. **Proven, not assumed**: removing the `location /` re-include drops index.html to 0 security headers with the server-level include still in place.

CSP `connect-src` is runtime-configured rather than derived from `DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY` — an authority carries a path, CSP matches by path prefix, and Azure AD's token endpoint sits outside it, so deriving it would have passed discovery then blocked the code exchange.

## #1388 — CloudFront absorbed nothing; no WAF

Caching was disabled on every path, so the CDN shed nothing — a flood and a page load cost the origin the same. The only limiter was the app's own, which counts inside the request path and **fails open**, so the pressure most likely to stress Redis is what disables it.

- WAFv2 ACL: per-IP rate ceiling (2000/5min, an order of magnitude above the app's 120/min class) + 8KB body cap. Viewer-IP aggregation, not `FORWARDED_IP` — nothing sits in front of the edge, so a forwarded header there is attacker-chosen.
- `/assets/*` cache behavior (safe only because filenames are content-hashed). `/api/*`, `/mcp`, `index.html` still always reach the origin.
- ~$7/mo; `waf_enabled = false` removes it.

- **Backend:** 4289 passed. The 6 new denial tests were run against the unfixed code and all 6 fail there, for the right reason.
- **Frontend:** 1034 passed, lint clean.
- **CSP in a real browser**, against the real built bundle behind the real nginx config (Vite dev never exercises this path): OTP sign-in, dashboard, results, assets, connections, suites, admin, profile, settings — **0 violations**; Monaco mounts and renders under `script-src 'self'`; module workers, blob workers and blob download URLs all allowed. Negative controls confirm the policy is *enforced*, not merely present — inline script, CDN script and cross-origin fetch are all blocked.
- **Terraform:** `validate` + `plan` against live AWS. 1 ACL created, CloudFront updated in place, Cognito flag flipped. No replacements.

## Rollout order (matters)

1. Merge, then `tofu apply` — this flips the Cognito flag and creates the WAF/caching.
2. `deploy-aws.yml` for the new images.
3. The task-def env additions (`OIDC_ALLOWED_*`, `DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC`) need `tofu apply -replace` + `update-service` — the task defs carry `ignore_changes[container_definitions]`, so a plain apply silently skips them (documented in the AWS README).
4. Azure needs a frontend redeploy to pick up `DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC`.

Verify after: sign-in still completes on both clouds (CSP touches the OIDC fetch path), and `/signup` on the Cognito domain no longer serves a form.

content.text: Finding #6 is the #802 collision class again. CloudFront patterns can't do regex, but they do support suffix wildcards — so I can mirror nginx's extension matching exactly:

input.old_string:
# Fingerprinted build output — the ONE thing here that is safe to cache at the
  # edge, and the only reason this distribution can absorb any load at all
  # (#1388). With caching disabled everywhere, every asset request on every page
  # load travelled the full CloudFront -> ALB -> nginx path, so the "CDN" in
  # front of the app shed nothing: an L7 flood and a legitimate page load cost
  # the origin exactly the same.
  #
  # Safe precisely because the filenames are content-hashed (nginx already serves
  # them `immutable`, frontend/nginx.conf.template): a changed asset is a changed
  # URL, so a long edge TTL can never serve a stale bundle. The path pattern
  # matches Vite's output directory.
  #
  # `/api/*`, `/mcp` and index.html are deliberately NOT given a behavior here —
  # they must keep hitting the origin every time.
  ordered_cache_behavior {
    path_pattern           = "/assets/*"
    target_origin_id       = "alb"
    viewer_protocol_policy = "redirect-to-https"
    allowed_methods        = ["GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"]
    cached_methods         = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    compress               = true

    # No origin_request_policy: AllViewer would forward every header and make the
    # cache key so specific that almost nothing would hit. CachingOptimized's own
    # key (URL only, plus normalized encoding) is what makes this cache work.
    cache_policy_id = data.aws_cloudfront_cache_policy.caching_optimized.id
  }

# Fingerprinted build output — the ONE thing here that is safe to cache at the
  # edge, and the only reason this distribution can absorb any load at all
  # (#1388). With caching disabled everywhere, every asset request on every page
  # load travelled the full CloudFront -> ALB -> nginx path, so the "CDN" in
  # front of the app shed nothing: an L7 flood and a legitimate page load cost
  # the origin exactly the same.
  #
  # Safe precisely because the filenames are content-hashed (nginx already serves
  # them `immutable`, frontend/nginx.conf.template): a changed asset is a changed
  # URL, so a long edge TTL can never serve a stale bundle.
  #
  # MATCHED BY EXTENSION, NOT BY THE `/assets/` PREFIX — deliberately, and this is
  # the same collision that produced #802. Vite emits its bundle to `dist/assets/`,
  # which shares a path prefix with the app's OWN `/assets/:assetId` SPA route
  # (the ADR 0034 asset browse). A `/assets/*` behavior captures that route too
  # and hands a *document* to a policy meant for immutable files; it happens not
  # to break today only because `location /` sends `no-cache` and CloudFront
  # honours it, i.e. correctness rests on an implicit dependency rather than on
  # the routing. nginx solved this by matching the file extension
  # (nginx.conf.template's `location ~*`), and this mirrors it. CloudFront
  # path patterns take `*`/`?` but no regex, hence one behavior per extension.
  #
  # `/api/*`, `/mcp` and index.html get no behavior here at all — they must keep
  # reaching the origin every time.
  dynamic "ordered_cache_behavior" {
    for_each = local.cacheable_asset_patterns
    content {
      path_pattern           = ordered_cache_behavior.value
      target_origin_id       = "alb"
      viewer_protocol_policy = "redirect-to-https"
      allowed_methods        = ["GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"]
      cached_methods         = ["GET", "HEAD"]
      compress               = true

      # No origin_request_policy: AllViewer would forward every header and make
      # the cache key so specific that almost nothing would hit. CachingOptimized's
      # own key (URL only, plus normalized encoding) is what makes this cache work.
      cache_policy_id = data.aws_cloudfront_cache_policy.caching_optimized.id
    }
  }

    """Whether `email` (already normalized) may hold a DataQ account via OIDC (#1386).

    Mirrors `otp_service.is_signup_eligible`, with one deliberate difference in the

    removed from the allowlist, so the list would grant access but never revoke

    longer be admitted.
    """
    # `_settings` (the module's import-time binding), not a fresh `get_settings()`
    # — every other read in this module goes through it, and one settings source
    # per module is what keeps a monkeypatched override from applying to half the

def _oidc_access_allowed(email: str, settings: Settings | None = None) -> bool:
    """Whether `email` (already normalized) may hold a DataQ account via OIDC (#1386).

    Mirrors `otp_service.is_signup_eligible`, with one deliberate difference in the
    empty-allowlist case: OTP treats "no allowlist" as *nobody* (and refuses to
    boot), while this returns True — see the `oidc_allowed_emails` field comment
    in `core/config.py` for why a fail-closed default here would turn a routine
    image bump into a workspace-wide lockout.

    Checked on EVERY request, not only at first provisioning. Gating just the
    insert would leave an already-provisioned identity in place after it is
    removed from the allowlist, so the list would grant access but never revoke
    it — this way it doubles as the kill-switch for an account that should no
    longer be admitted.

    `settings` is explicit (same shape as `is_signup_eligible`) because the THREE
    callers do not share one settings source: the two REST dependencies read this
    module's import-time `_settings`, while `mcp.auth` resolves its own via
    `get_settings()`. They are the same object in a running process, but letting
    each caller pass what it already holds is what keeps /mcp and /api from
    diverging under a test override — which is precisely how the /mcp path came
    to be missed in the first place.
    """
    s = settings or _settings
    if not s.oidc_allowlist_configured:
        return True
    if email in s.oidc_allowed_email_set:
        return True
    _, _, domain = email.partition("@")
    return bool(domain) and domain in s.oidc_allowed_domain_set

fix: address the six /code-review findings on this PR

The important one: **/mcp was still ungated.** `_resolve_generic_oidc_user`
unified the two REST dependencies, but `mcp/auth.py`'s `resolve_current_user`
is a THIRD generic-OIDC resolver calling `_upsert_user` directly — so a token
the REST API 403s authenticated fine at /mcp, was provisioned a users row, and
got all 8 tools including `trigger_suite_run`. That is the exact invariant the
Azure-guest branch a few lines below states out loud, and it defeated the
point of the fix. `_oidc_access_allowed` now takes an explicit `settings`
(mirroring `is_signup_eligible`) because the three callers genuinely do not
share one settings source — letting each pass what it already holds is what
stops /mcp and /api drifting again. Verified: both new denial tests fail
against the ungated code.

Also:

- The denial was undiagnosable. `email=` is in `_PII_KEYS`, so it logged as
  redacted, and the 403 body deliberately doesn't echo the address either — a
  misconfigured allowlist had no diagnosable surface anywhere. `_denied_identity`
  logs the domain plus a stable digest. My own test then caught that the digest
  wasn't canonical, which would have quietly broken the one property it exists
  for (an operator reproducing it from an address a user gives them), so it
  normalizes internally rather than trusting the caller.

- The 8KB edge body cap plausibly blocked `POST /suites/import`, and a WAF block
  happens at the edge: no origin log, no request id, nothing the user can report.
  A security control whose false positive is invisible is worse than one slightly
  wider, so that path is scoped out and left to nginx's 1MB cap.

- `waf_max_body_bytes` is now range-validated below 16384. WAF inspects at most
  16KB of a CloudFront body, so a larger threshold makes the rule unmatchable
  while still showing as enabled — the apply now fails instead.

- `/assets/*` was a prefix match that also captured the app's own
  `/assets/:assetId` SPA route — the same collision as #802. It only worked via
  an implicit dependency on `location /`'s no-cache, and contradicted the
  comment claiming index.html always reaches the origin. Now matched by
  extension, mirroring what nginx already does.

- Moved the OIDC-allowlist doc block (including its PII warning) back onto the
  variables it documents; the WAF section header had orphaned it onto
  `waf_enabled`.

## Network exposure

- The **frontend is the only public surface**; the API runs on **internal ingress** and is
  reached only through the frontend's same-origin `/api`, `/healthz`, and `/mcp` proxy
  (ADR 0028 §5). All traffic is over **HTTPS/TLS**.
- The **MCP** AI-assistant endpoint is **fail-closed** — unauthenticated requests are rejected
  (ADR 0008), and it is not mounted at all unless the deployment has a working sign-in
  configuration. It authenticates from the `Authorization` header only and **never reads a
  cookie**, so a signed-in browser lured to a hostile page cannot be used to drive it.
  In an **OTP-only** deployment there is no identity provider, so a **PAT is the only
  credential MCP accepts**: a session token is rejected by prefix before any validation, and
  a bearer that is neither is rejected outright rather than handed to an unconfigured
  validator — the absence of a JWT verifier is a refusal, never a skipped check.
- **CSRF.** The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`, which blocks cross-site POSTs; that only
  holds while every state-changing endpoint is a POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE, so the test suite
  audits the whole route table for a GET that mutates. Sign-in and sign-out are both POST-only,
  and the SPA and API share an origin through the proxy, so a cross-site request can neither
  carry nor read the cookie.
- **Two coordinated auth-mode selectors.** The frontend's runtime `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE` and the
  backend's inferred mode (SSO variables, or the OTP mailer + allowlist block) are separate
  contracts — neither can derive the other. Set them together; the full table is in
  [`deploy/README.md`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/deploy/README.md) and
  [`.env.app.example`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/.env.app.example). The
  backend refuses to start on a half-configured OTP block rather than come up unable to log
  anybody in.

## Secrets

- Datasource credentials, webhook signing keys, and channel secrets are held in a **secret
  store behind a seam** — Azure Key Vault in the primary reference deployment, AWS Secrets
  Manager on the AWS stack, OpenBao/Vault self-hosted — never in the database or in git. The
  app reads them via a managed identity (Azure) or the task IAM role (AWS).
- Secret **references** (names), not secret values, are stored alongside connections. Deleting
  a connection removes its secret (soft-delete on Key Vault).
- Inbound webhooks are authenticated: ADF by a shared secret, Airflow and dbt by an
  **HMAC-SHA256** signature keyed on a stored signing key.

## The data DataQ sees, stores, and redacts

DataQ runs checks *against* your data; it is **not** a copy of your data. What it persists:

- **Metadata** — suites, checks, connection config (no secrets), schedules, trigger bindings.
- **Results** — per-check pass/fail + a numeric `metric_value`, and for failing checks a
  small **failing-row sample**.
- **Failing-row samples are the one place results can carry PII/PHI.** They are **redacted at
  the boundary, column-aware**: a suite's **column policy** (auto-derived by a classifier or
  set by hand) keeps non-sensitive breach values debuggable while masking PII columns to
  `<redacted>`. The numeric counts and row/column shape are kept.
- **Logs & traces** are PII-redacted at the logger level, and secret values never enter them.

## Retention

- Failing-row **samples are purged** after a retention window (PII-minimisation), while the
  aggregatable **`metric_value` history is kept** for trends and baselines — so you lose the
  raw rows but keep the signal.

## Encryption

- **In transit:** HTTPS/TLS everywhere (public ingress and the internal proxy hop).
- **At rest:** provided by the managed data services — PostgreSQL, the object stores, and the
  secret store (Key Vault / AWS Secrets Manager) all encrypt at rest in both reference
  deployments.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please report suspected security issues privately to the maintainers rather than opening a
public issue.

## Authentication & access

- **Single sign-on (OIDC).** Users sign in through your identity provider; DataQ is
  provider-neutral (validated against Azure AD). The backend validates the token on every
  request — there is no local password store.
- **Personal access tokens (PATs).** For headless / AI-client use, users mint `dq_live_`
  tokens ([API keys](api-keys.md)). Tokens are **hashed (SHA-256) at rest** — the plaintext is
  shown once and never stored — and carry the **same authz as the user**, on REST and MCP.
  They can be scoped with an expiry and revoked.
- **Email one-time codes (OTP).** For deployments with **no identity provider**, a human can
  sign in by proving they own a mailbox: DataQ mails a 6-digit code, and verifying it sets an
  **HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax** session cookie (fixed lifetime, default 24 h, **no refresh
  token** — signing in again is the refresh). Logout revokes the session server-side, and both
  expiry and revocation are checked on every request. Sessions are hashed (SHA-256) at rest,
  like PATs. Sign-up is **allowlist-only** — there is no open registration. MCP does **not**
  accept a session: it is a browser credential, and PATs remain the headless credential

input.new_string:
- **Single sign-on (OIDC).** Users sign in through your identity provider; DataQ is
  provider-neutral (validated against Azure AD and AWS Cognito). The backend validates the

- **Who may hold an account is your decision, not your IdP's.** DataQ provisions a user on
  first successful sign-in, so without a gate the identity provider's *registration* policy
  silently becomes DataQ's *access* policy. That is fine for an invite-only tenant and wrong
  for a provider with self-service sign-up. Two independent controls:
  - Keep the identity provider invite-only (the AWS reference stack sets
    `allow_admin_create_user_only` on the Cognito pool; an Azure AD tenant is invite-only by
    nature).
  - Set `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS` / `OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` as the app-side allowlist. It is
    checked on **every request**, not only at first sign-in, so removing an entry revokes an
    existing account rather than merely blocking a new one.

  Leaving the allowlist empty means "admit anyone the issuer vouches for" — deliberately, so
  that upgrading DataQ can never lock an existing workspace out — and the API logs
  `auth_oidc_no_signup_allowlist` at **WARNING** on every boot in that state. If you see that
  line, confirm your IdP is invite-only.

## AWS reference deployment

The same product deploys to AWS from the in-repo OpenTofu stack
([`deploy/terraform/aws/`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/tree/main/deploy/terraform/aws)) —
identical images, identical topology, each seam pointed at the AWS implementation:

```
Browser ──HTTPS──► CloudFront (public surface, origin secret verified at nginx)
                   ▼
              ALB ──► frontend (ECS Fargate, nginx + SPA) ──proxies──► api (ECS Fargate)
                   │  api/worker sidecars: ADOT collector → X-Ray traces + CloudWatch logs
                   ├──► RDS PostgreSQL          ├──► ElastiCache Redis (TLS)
                   ├──► AWS Secrets Manager     └──► SES (email alerts)
              Cognito (OIDC issuer for the SPA + API)
```

- **Secrets:** `SECRET_STORE=aws_secrets_manager` (fourth store behind the seam).
- **Auth:** Amazon Cognito through the same generic OIDC contract (`DATAQ_AUTH_*`,
  `AUTH_OIDC_*`) — the second issuer validated in a real deployment after Azure AD. Cognito
  needs `DATAQ_AUTH_LOGOUT_STYLE=cognito` (its `/logout` is not RP-Initiated-Logout
  conformant) and resolves the user profile via the **userinfo endpoint** (its access tokens
  carry neither `email` nor `aud`).
- **Observability:** the app's vendor-neutral OTLP export feeds an **ADOT collector sidecar**
  → X-Ray traces + OpenTelemetry logs in CloudWatch with matching trace ids.
- **Deploy:** a parallel **Deploy (AWS)** workflow (`deploy-aws.yml`) — GitHub OIDC role
  login, immutable `aws-<sha>` tags, migrate run-task gated on exit 0, then ECS service
  rolls and a CloudFront smoke.
- **Gotchas** (full list in the
  [AWS README](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/blob/main/deploy/terraform/aws/README.md)):
  a `rediss://` broker URL needs `ssl_cert_reqs` (the app now defaults it to `required`);

  `tofu apply -replace`; CloudFront sends an **origin secret header** that nginx enforces,
  so a third-party distribution cannot origin-point at the ALB.

  as admits). Leaving the allowlist empty is permitted and logs

  limiter (which fails open by design), plus edge caching of the fingerprinted bundle. Set
  `waf_enabled = false` to opt out of the ~$7/month.
- **Browser security headers** ship with the frontend image on every deployment. Narrow the
  CSP's `connect-src` to your identity provider's origins with `DATAQ_CSP_CONNECT_SRC` — for
  Cognito that is **two** hosts (the issuer for discovery/JWKS, the hosted-UI domain for the
  token exchange); the permissive `https:` default keeps sign-in working if you don't.

 "**/code-review then caught the fix's own blind spot: a THIRD generic-OIDC resolver.** Unifying the two REST dependencies was not enough — `mcp/auth.py`'s `resolve_current_user` called `_upsert_user` directly, so a token the REST API 403s authenticated at `/mcp` and got all 8 tools incl. `trigger_suite_run`, breaking the invariant that file's own Azure-guest branch states out loud. "
 "**#1387:** ZERO security response headers on either cloud (repo-wide grep found none defined anywhere). The trap: nginx drops inherited `add_header` at any level declaring its own, and three locations set `Cache-Control` — including `location /`, which serves index.html — so a server-level block would have been silently absent from exactly the response that needs a CSP, while looking correct in the config. **Proven, not assumed:** removing the `location /` re-include drops index.html to 0 headers with the server-level include still present. CSP `connect-src` is a separate runtime var, NOT derived from `DATAQ_AUTH_AUTHORITY` — an authority carries a path, CSP matches by path prefix, and Azure AD's token endpoint sits outside it; live AWS confirmed the same shape from the other direction (token endpoint `…auth.us-east-2.amazoncognito.com` is a DIFFERENT host from JWKS `cognito-idp…`, so Cognito needs BOTH). Image default is `https:` not empty, so a BYO upgrade can't silently break sign-in. "
 "**#1388:** CloudFront ran `CachingDisabled` on every path — a pure pass-through absorbing nothing — in front of an in-app limiter that **fails open**, i.e. the pressure most likely to hurt Redis is what disables it. Added a WAF per-IP ceiling (2000/5min) + an 8KB body cap (import path scoped out: a WAF block happens at the edge, so its false positive has no origin log at all) and extension-matched `/assets/*.<ext>` edge caching — **not** the `/assets/*` prefix, which review caught would re-collide with the SPA's own `/assets/:assetId` route (#802 class). "
 "**Deployed to both clouds on `92c97b8c`** — Azure [run 31933670333](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/actions/runs/31933670333) + AWS [run 31933647024](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/actions/runs/31933647024), both green. Live-verified after: headers went **0 → 6 on both** (`server:` no longer leaks the version); CSP enforcing in prod (inline script, CDN script and `http:` connect all blocked) with the app rendering and Azure AD discovery+JWKS reachable; **the exploit is dead two ways** — hosted `/signup` now 302s with no form, and `aws cognito-idp sign-up` returns `NotAuthorizedException: SignUp is not permitted for this user pool`; WAF attached with 60/60 normal requests unaffected; edge caching Miss→**Hit** on a fingerprinted asset while `/assets/<uuid>` stays uncached `text/html`, proving the collision fix. "
 "**Left open by choice:** [#1384](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1384) (CloudFront→ALB hop is cleartext — needs a custom domain + ACM; this also made the published docs' \"HTTPS/TLS everywhere\" claim an overclaim, now corrected) and [#1385](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1385) (ElastiCache at-rest encryption off beside an encrypted RDS; unrestricted egress from all subnets — the exfil path #1118 would use). **Azure still has no WAF equivalent and neither cloud autoscales** — both recorded in #1388.")

content.text:
Done. Here's where everything landed.

## What shipped

Three fixes ([#1389](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1389)), deployed to both clouds on `92c97b8c` — Azure [run 31933670333](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/actions/runs/31933670333), AWS [run 31933647024](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/actions/runs/31933647024), both green.

**#1386 — the live-exploitable one is closed.** Verified dead two independent ways: the hosted `/signup` now returns 302 with no form, and the API rejects registration outright (`NotAuthorizedException: SignUp is not permitted for this user pool`). The app-side allowlist is active on the deployed API — its boot log reads `signup_allowlist: true`.

**#1387 — headers went 0 → 6 on both clouds**, verified against the running sites (baseline captured beforehand was 0). CSP is *enforcing*, not just present: inline script, CDN script and `http:` connect are all blocked in prod, while the app renders and every IdP endpoint stays reachable.

**#1388 — WAF attached, edge caching working.** A fingerprinted asset now goes Miss→**Hit**; `/assets/<uuid>` correctly stays uncached HTML. 60/60 normal requests unaffected.

## Two things worth flagging

**The review caught a hole that defeated my own fix.** I unified the two REST OIDC resolvers, but `/mcp` was a *third* one — a token the REST API 403s would have authenticated there and received all 8 tools including `trigger_suite_run`. Both new denial tests were confirmed to fail against the ungated code. Five other findings fixed in the same pass.

**I corrected a published claim this audit disproved.** `docs/security.md` said "HTTPS/TLS everywhere"; that was false — the AWS CloudFront→ALB hop is cleartext. The site now names both plaintext internal hops and distinguishes the contained one from the real one. Same for at-rest encryption, which omitted the ElastiCache exception.

## Docs

`security.md`, `deployment.md`, `deployment-parity.md`, `compliance-posture.md`, `changelog.md`, `progress.md`, and CLAUDE.md §13. GitHub Pages is live and verified — the old claim is gone, the new sections are published.

## Filed, not fixed

- [#1384](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1384) — cleartext origin hop; needs a custom domain + ACM.
- [#1385](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1385) — ElastiCache at-rest encryption off; unrestricted egress (the exfil path #1118 would use).

## Two things you should decide on

**Azure has no WAF equivalent**, and this work makes that asymmetric: AWS now sheds floods at the edge, Azure has only the in-app limiter — which fails open. Front Door + WAF is the analogous change; I've noted it in #1388 rather than acting, since it's a cost decision on the primary prod during a wind-down question.

**Cognito MFA is still off.** Fine for an invite-only demo pool, but it's a live choice rather than a default now.

One caveat on my own verification: I could not complete an interactive browser sign-in on either cloud (no cached session, and I wouldn't ask for credentials). I verified the CSP permits every request the OIDC flow makes — discovery, JWKS, and the token host — with a negative control proving the policy is genuinely narrowed. That's strong, but it isn't the same as a full round-trip login, so it's worth you clicking through once.
